newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-British stocks seen consolidating in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-British stocks seen consolidating in '97.

text.p: Britain's stock market looks set to consolidate next year despite concern over interest rates rising, according to a Reuters survey of forecasts for the world's top 15 bourses.
Most analysts said they were not unduly concerned about a possible Labour Party victory in a general election, which must be held by next May.

The average forecast of analysts polled by Reuters showed the benchmark FTSE 100 index ending 1997 at 4,250 points, up by more than five percent from its current level. The index closed on Tuesday at 4,035.
The highest prediction in the poll was 4,500 and the lowest was 4,000.

Brokerage houses mostly expected economic growth to sustain share prices in the coming year, although some analysts doubted that the gains of 1996 could be matched as inflation could take off and lead to tighter monetary policy.
Following are a selection of views on next year's performance of top London shares:
IAN SCOTT, EUROPEAN EQUITY STRATEGIST, LEHMAN BROS

"The thing that makes us probably more nervous is that we're unlikely to get much clarity in terms of the policies which (the Labour party) is likely to pursue once in power. I don't think the pre-election period will throw a lot of light on the precise details of policies."
ANDY HARTWILL, BRITISH EQUITY STRATEGIST, SGST
"Next year will be dominated by low growth, low earnings growth, concerns over Europe in particular and expectations that the European recovery will pick up."
IAN WILLIAMS, EQUITY STRATEGIST, PANMURE GORDON
"When the strength of the domestic economy does come through next year, there's actually a potential for upgrades as we move through the year."
GARY DUGAN, EUROPEAN EQUITY MARKET STRATEGIST, J.P. MORGAN

"It is difficult to talk about positive factors in an election year in the UK. But the economy is showing very robust growth. We've got about 3.7 percent GDP growth next year, which we think will translate into good corporate profits growth."
